title: What You Get When You Lead Like a Servant (and What You Lose If You Don’t)
author: Joel Salinas
summary: Joel Salinas and Chris Russo argue that servant leadership, though slower and less visible, outperforms power-centered leadership over time. They ground the claim in James Hunter's The Servant and in Mark 10, and say the point holds for readers who do not share their Christian faith. They list three gains: trust that outlives tenure, people who own the mission, and resilience in transition. They then list three losses for leaders who refuse to serve: credibility, influence, and spiritual anchoring. The piece closes with a TL;DR and a self-check asking whether the reader leads to serve or to be seen. The argument rests on the authors' observation and conviction rather than on cited data, and the faith framing is explicit.
points: Power-based leadership yields short-term productivity but leaves burnt bridges, while servant leadership builds loyalty, ownership and a lasting culture.
The authors name three concrete gains: trust that outlives the leader, a team that owns the mission, and a relational foundation that holds up when change arrives.
The cost of not serving is that teams learn to protect themselves from the leader, so honesty gives way to silence and commitment to compliance.
They argue that wanting remote staff back in the office mainly for control signals a trust deficit, not leadership.
The self-check asks whether the leader is leading to serve or to be seen, and whether the team would say they left a legacy.
quotes: In fast-moving leadership cultures, servant leadership can feel like a liability. It’s slower. Less visible. Often, less rewarded, at least in the short term.

The short-term gains of power-centered leadership are a boost in productivity or in quick gains, but are usually short-lived and leaving burnt bridges behind. But servant leadership? It builds loyalty. It fosters ownership. It creates cultures that don't just function but flourish.

Servant leaders don’t need to micromanage because their team trusts their WHY. Over time, that kind of trust creates a psychological safety net that produces innovation and candid feedback, two things you cannot buy with incentives.

When people are served, not used, they don’t just show up for the paycheck or the perks. They show up with purpose, with drive. They defend the culture. They protect the values. They take personal responsibility for results. These are the cornerstones for long-term, successful performance of a team.

Power-based leadership may seem effective in the short term, but over time, teams learn to protect themselves from you, not follow you. Silence replaces honesty. Compliance replaces commitment. Eventually, disconnection takes over, and people leave.

If people only follow you when you’re watching, you haven’t built leadership; that’s just surveillance. If the only reason you want your remote team back in an office where you can see them is for closer control, then trust may be the main deficiency. Real influence happens when people internalize the mission, not when they fear the presence of the leader.

As a leader, you must recognize the value of those you lead and lift them up. Only then will you be able to lead the team as a whole to your goal, while creating a sustainable, scalable system that will last.
